name: Power analysis
seoDesc: Power analysis: work out group 1 (hidden) from the group 1 and the group 2. A free statistics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Power analysis calculator the group 1, the group 2, the enrollment ratio and the alpha and it returns group 1 (hidden). It is built for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Power analysis calculator work?
sections.html:
The Power analysis calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports group 1 (hidden) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the study group design, the primary endpoint and the effect size (Two groups & dichotomous endpoint)); then you type in the group 1 (Two groups & dichotomous endpoint), the group 2 (Two groups & dichotomous endpoint), the enrollment ratio (Two groups & dichotomous endpoint) and the alpha (Two groups & dichotomous endpoint).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Power analysis calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Group 1=(group 1, (group 1, group 2, effect size), alpha, power, enrollment ratio)
Group 2=(group 1, (group 1, group 2, effect size), alpha, power, enrollment ratio)
Group2helper=(group 1, group 2, effect size)
Total=((group 1, (group 1, group 2, effect size), alpha, power, enrollment ratio) + (group 1, (group 1, group 2, effect size), alpha, power, enrollment ratio))
N 1 case 2=(known population, (known population, study group, effect size), alpha, power)
Prop 2 case 2=(known population, study group, effect size)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Study group design set to Two independent study group, Primary endpoint set to Dichotomous (yes/no), Effect size set to Incidence (absolute value) and Enrollment ratio = 1. The calculator returns Group 2 (mean) = 10.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Group 2 (mean) = 10 should be roughly the size you expected from Study group design set to Two independent study group and Primary endpoint set to Dichotomous (yes/no).

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Power analysis calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the group 1, the group 2 and the enrollment ratio — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Power analysis calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns group 1 (hidden), derived from the group 1, the group 2 and the enrollment ratio. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Power analysis calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the group 1, the group 2, the enrollment ratio and the alpha, which is 25 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter group 1 (Two groups & dichotomous endpoint) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Group 1 (Two groups & dichotomous endpoint) opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (6 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Group 2 (mean) = 10. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Power analysis calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
